chunks: Al-Bazofari from Ahmad ibn Idris from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who died and left behind a pregnant slave girl and two male slaves, so a brother of his inherited them. He freed the two slaves, and the slave girl gave birth to a boy. After the manumission, they testified that their master had made them witnesses that he used to have intercourse with the slave girl and that the pregnancy was from him. He said: 'Their testimony is valid, and they are returned as slaves as they were.'

Because the first report is based on recommendation (istihbab), and the last report is based on the fact that it is permissible for the child to enslave them, because he who freed them was one who did not own them. However, it is recommended for him to free them inasmuch as they established his lineage, and there is no contradiction between the two in any case.
From him (Al-Bazofari) from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Ahmad ibn Ziyad from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him)

He said: I asked him about a man upon whom death is approaching, and he has slaves for his own exclusive possession, and he has slaves in partnership with another man. He bequeaths in his will that his slaves are free. What is the status of his slaves who are in partnership? He wrote to him (peace be upon him): 'They are appraised against him; if his wealth can bear the cost, then they are free.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on freeing partnership slaves in a will and the validity of their testimony for establishing lineage?
ai.summary: This passage from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the nuances of partial manumission (*'itq al-nusuf* or similar contexts) and the validity of testimony by co-owned slaves, emphasizing that while their testimony establishing lineage is accepted, they revert to slavery as the manumitter lacked full ownership, though it is recommended to free them for the sake of lineage. The second narration addresses the bequest of partnership slaves, ruling that they are appraised against the estate and become free only if the testator's remaining wealth can cover their value, reflecting the Shia juristic principle of protecting heirs' rights while honoring the dying man's wish. These rulings highlight the interplay between property rights, lineage verification, and the spiritual merit of manumission in Shia fiqh.
